reason: The text demonstrates a clear progression toward antagonism. While the men of Shechem initially support Abimelech and make him king (וַיַּמְלִ֥יכוּ אֶת־ אֲבִימֶ֖לֶךְ), the narrative explicitly states that God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, causing them to 'deal treacherously with him' (וַיִּבְגְּד֥וּ בַעֲלֵי־ שְׁכֶ֖ם בַּאֲבִימֶֽלֶךְ). Subsequently, they transfer their allegiance to Gaal son of Ebed, with Gaal openly questioning why they should serve Abimelech (מִֽי־ אֲבִימֶ֤לֶךְ וּמִֽי־ שְׁכֶם כִּ֣י נַעַבְדֶ֔נּוּ). The people engage in armed conflict against Abimelech, ultimately defending the tower of Shechem against his siege. This extended narrative arc clearly shows the regular people becoming and remaining antagonistic toward their leader.
